anchors.hint: the incoming axon/nerve fiber carrying the electrical signal into the terminal
the swollen end of the axon (the synaptic knob) where neurotransmitter is stored and released
mitochondrion inside the terminal, supplying ATP for the energy-demanding release process
voltage-gated calcium channel in the presynaptic membrane that opens when the action potential arrives
a synaptic vesicle storing neurotransmitter molecules before release
a vesicle fusing with the presynaptic membrane to release neurotransmitter (exocytosis)
the presynaptic cell membrane the vesicle fuses with
the fluid-filled gap the neurotransmitter diffuses across
an enzyme in the cleft (e.g. acetylcholinesterase) that breaks down neurotransmitter to stop the signal
the membrane of the next neuron, containing receptors
a receptor protein neurotransmitter binds to, opening an ion channel on the postsynaptic side
the next neuron/cell receiving and propagating the signal onward

templates.name: Nephron Cross-Section
templates.description: A labeled cross-section of a single nephron (renal corpuscle, proximal/distal convoluted tubules, loop of Henle, collecting duct) with the surrounding blood supply. Use for content describing kidney/nephron structure, ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, urine formation, or the role of ADH in water reabsorption.

anchors.hint: the vessel bringing blood into the glomerulus from the renal artery; wider than the efferent arteriole, which raises blood pressure inside the glomerulus

the tangled capillary knot inside Bowman's capsule; high blood pressure here forces water, ions, glucose, and other small molecules out of the blood (ultrafiltration) — blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass through and stay in the blood
the cup-shaped capsule surrounding the glomerulus that collects the filtered fluid and funnels it into the tubule
the vessel carrying blood out of the glomerulus; narrower than the afferent arteriole, which keeps pressure inside the glomerulus high enough to keep filtering
the first coiled section of the tubule, where most reabsorption happens — essentially all glucose and amino acids, and most water, sodium and other ions, are reabsorbed back into the blood here
the descending limb of the loop of Henle; its wall is permeable to water, so as filtrate flows down into the increasingly salty medulla, water is drawn out by osmosis, concentrating the filtrate
the bend of the loop of Henle deep in the medulla, where the surrounding tissue fluid is most concentrated and the filtrate reaches its highest solute concentration

the ascending limb of the loop of Henle; its wall is impermeable to water but actively pumps sodium and chloride out into the surrounding tissue, diluting the filtrate and building the salt gradient that lets the collecting duct reabsorb water later
the second coiled section of the tubule, where further, hormonally-regulated reabsorption and secretion fine-tune the composition of the filtrate

the duct filtrate flows through on its way out of the kidney; antidiuretic hormone (ADH) makes its wall more permeable to water when the body needs to conserve water, so more water is reabsorbed here and less, more concentrated urine is produced
the network of capillaries wrapped around the tubule that picks up everything reabsorbed along the way and carries it back into the general blood circulation

templates.name: Neuron Structure & Reflex Arc
templates.description: A two-part labeled diagram: the top half shows a full spinal reflex arc (receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron in the spinal cord, motor neuron, effector muscle); the bottom half is a zoomed-in single neuron showing dendrites, cell body, axon hillock, a myelinated axon with nodes of Ranvier, and the axon terminal. Use for content describing neuron structure, nerve impulse propagation, myelination/saltatory conduction, or reflex arcs/reflex actions — not for a single synapse/neurotransmitter-release mechanism, which belongs on the `synapse` template instead.

anchors.hint: the sensory receptor in the skin that detects the stimulus (e.g. heat, pain, pressure) and generates a nerve impulse
the sensory (afferent) neuron carrying the impulse from the receptor toward the spinal cord
the relay neuron inside the spinal cord connecting the sensory neuron directly to a motor neuron — this direct spinal connection, bypassing the brain, is what makes a reflex fast and involuntary
the motor (efferent) neuron carrying the impulse from the spinal cord out to the effector
the muscle (or gland) that receives the motor neuron's signal and responds — here, contracting to pull away from the stimulus
branching extensions that receive incoming signals from other neurons and carry them toward the cell body
the cell body (soma), containing the nucleus, where incoming signals are integrated
the trigger zone where an action potential is initiated once incoming signals reach threshold
the fatty insulating layer (formed by Schwann cells) wrapped around sections of the axon; it speeds up conduction by preventing ion leakage along the covered stretches

a gap in the myelin sheath where the axon membrane is exposed; the impulse 'jumps' from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is why myelinated axons conduct impulses much faster than unmyelinated ones
the branched end of the axon where the impulse arrives and triggers neurotransmitter release to the next cell (as in the synapse template)

templates.name: Plant vs Animal Cell (Organelles)
templates.description: A side-by-side comparison of an animal cell and a plant cell with organelles labeled across both: nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, and centrioles on the animal side; cell wall, chloroplasts, the large central vacuole, Golgi apparatus, and cytoplasm on the plant side. Several organelles (nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi) exist in both cell types even though only labeled on one side here — the hint for each anchor says so. Use for content describing general cell structure, organelle function, or comparing plant and animal cells — not for a detailed single-organelle deep-dive (e.g. mitochondrion internal structure, chloroplast light/dark reactions), which would need its own template.

anchors.hint: the selectively permeable membrane controlling what enters and leaves the cell — present in both animal and plant cells, though in a plant cell it sits just inside the rigid cell wall
contains the cell's genetic material (DNA) and controls cell activity — present in both animal and plant cells; in a mature plant cell it's often pushed to one side by the large central vacuole
the site of aerobic respiration, producing most of the cell's ATP — present in both animal and plant cells
a folded network of membranes that transports proteins and lipids around the cell — present in both animal and plant cells
a pair of structures that organize spindle fibres during cell division — found in animal cells, typically absent from plant cells
the site of protein synthesis, found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum — present in both animal and plant cells
the rigid outer layer made of cellulose, found in plant cells but not animal cells — gives the cell a fixed shape and structural support

a large, permanent, fluid-filled sac that takes up most of a mature plant cell's volume (unlike the small, temporary vacuoles sometimes seen in animal cells) — maintains the turgor pressure that keeps the plant cell rigid
contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis — found in plant cells (and algae), never in animal cells
a stack of flattened membranes that modifies, packages, and ships proteins and lipids to their destination — present in both animal and plant cells
the jelly-like fluid filling the cell outside the nucleus and vacuole, where many organelles sit and metabolic reactions take place

templates.name: Alveolus & Gas Exchange
templates.description: A two-part labeled diagram of gas exchange in the lungs: the top half shows an alveolar cluster fed by a bronchiole and wrapped in a capillary network, with the pulmonary artery bringing deoxygenated blood in and the pulmonary vein carrying oxygenated blood away; the bottom half is a zoomed cross-section of the alveolus-capillary interface showing the two thin cell layers, a red blood cell, and oxygen and carbon dioxide diffusing in opposite directions across the membrane. Use for content describing gas exchange, alveoli/lung structure, or the structural adaptations for efficient diffusion — not for the mechanics of breathing/ventilation itself (chest cavity, diaphragm, intercostal muscles), which would need its own template.

anchors.hint: the small airway that carries fresh, oxygen-rich air from the bronchioles into the alveoli

brings deoxygenated blood (low O2, high CO2) from the heart to the lungs to be reoxygenated
carries newly oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart, to be pumped around the body
the alveolus wall is only one cell thick (a flattened Type I pneumocyte) — a structural adaptation that keeps the diffusion path as short as possible
a fluid secreted by Type II pneumocytes that reduces surface tension inside the alveolus, stopping it from collapsing as air moves in and out
the capillary wall is also just one cell thick (endothelium), so together with the alveolus wall the total diffusion path between air and blood is only two cells wide
carries oxygen bound to haemoglobin; red blood cells pass through the capillary in single file, which maximises the time each one spends next to the alveolus wall for gas exchange
oxygen diffuses from the alveolus air space, where its concentration is high, into the blood, where it's lower — down its concentration gradient
carbon dioxide diffuses the opposite way: from the blood, where its concentration is high, into the alveolus air space, to be breathed out — down its own concentration gradient
